articleBlocks: Initially, seeing clues like Titan and Triton, I immediately jumped to Greek mythology.
Phobos seemed to fit that theme, too.
Io didn't quite click as a mythological figure, and I started to doubt my initial read.
Then I noticed the clue "Ganymede (seen by Galileo).".
The answer is moons in our solar system.
Each clue represents a moon orbiting a planet in our celestial neighborhood.
In hindsight, the mythological names are a bit of a red herring; they're just the source of the moon names.
The puzzle demonstrates how crucial it is to stay open to new interpretations as more clues become available.
solutionNarrative: Titan and Triton first pulled me toward greek gods, so that was the first path I tested. It held together for a moment, but ganymede (seen by Galileo) never really fit it. The more I pushed that first read, the more the board sounded stitched together instead of naturally solved.

The solve turned when I stopped treating ganymede (seen by Galileo) as just another clue and asked what kind of thing each clue could really be describing. Once I made that shift, I was no longer thinking about greek gods; I was checking whether the earlier clues all behaved like parts of the same real set. That was when the answer became clear, because the remaining clues stopped feeling like separate trivia and started reinforcing the real category.
